content: In southern India, the sexual identity of men who have sex with men (MSM) is often associated with their role in anal intercourse. However, there is limited understanding of how sexual mixing occurs between different identity groups. Both role segregation and assortative mixing (within-group mixing) are known to influence the size of HIV epidemics in various settings. This study aimed to investigate how different patterns of sexual mixing impact estimated HIV trends and the effectiveness of interventions targeting MSM in Bangalore. Deterministic models were developed to describe HIV transmission among three MSM identity groups: predominantly insertive panthis/bisexuals (PB), predominantly receptive kothis/hijras (KH), and versatile double-deckers (DD). These models were parameterized using data collected in Bangalore as part of the evaluation of the Avahan intervention. The models explored four distinct mixing patterns and used 300,000 randomly sampled parameter sets derived from data ranges to identify multiple fits to group-specific HIV prevalence data from 2006 and 2009. These model fits were then used to compare predicted HIV time trends. To assess the impact of a new intervention scenario, it was assumed that condom use would decline from high levels in 2010 due to intervention fatigue. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) was introduced in 2015, with an assumed effectiveness of 42% (efficacy multiplied by adherence) and 60% coverage, targeting KH and DD groups, which were considered the easiest to reach. The results showed significant differences in levels of assortative mixing for fits identified using different mixing patterns. However, there was minimal projected difference in HIV prevalence trends across these patterns. The overall impact of PrEP on the entire MSM population was similar, with less than a 10% difference in the percentage of infections averted. The study concluded that a variety of mixing patterns are consistent with the data. However, model predictions of future HIV epidemic trends and the overall impact of targeted interventions are robust to the different mixing patterns and intervention scenarios explored. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) used as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) by HIV-seronegative individuals reduces the risk of acquiring HIV. However, the population-level impact and cost-effectiveness of using PrEP as a public health intervention remain debated. A stochastic agent-based model of HIV transmission and progression was used to simulate clinical and cost outcomes of different PrEP strategies for MSM in New South Wales (NSW), Australia. Outcomes were reported as incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) in 2013 Australian dollars per quality-adjusted life year gained (QALYG). The use of PrEP in 10-30% of the entire NSW MSM population was projected to cost an additional $316-952 million over 10 years, with costs exceeding $400,000 per QALYG compared to the status quo. Targeting MSM with more than 10 to more than 50 sexual partners within six months cost an additional $31-331 million, with costs exceeding $110,000 per QALYG compared to the status quo. PrEP was found to be most cost-effective when targeted at HIV-negative MSM in discordant regular partnerships, with ICERs ranging from $8,399 to $11,575 for coverage levels between 15% and 30%. The study concluded that targeting HIV-negative MSM in discordant regular partnerships is a cost-effective intervention. However, this highly targeted strategy would not have a large population-level impact. Other scenarios are unlikely to be cost-effective. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed recommendations for the use of daily oral antiretrovirals in HIV-uninfected individuals to prevent HIV acquisition, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Evidence is available from studies involving two groups: MSM and transgender women who have sex with men, and serodiscordant heterosexual couples. These recommendations aim to inform the use of PrEP in demonstration projects and provide guidance on its implementation. In the United States, an estimated 48,100 new HIV infections occurred in 2009, with 27% in heterosexual men and women who did not inject drugs and 64% in MSM, including 3% in MSM who inject drugs. Following evidence of the safety and efficacy of daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) as PrEP in the iPrEx trial, the CDC issued interim guidance for its use among MSM. Since then, data from studies of PrEP among heterosexual men and women have become available, and the FDA approved a label indication for reducing the risk of sexual HIV acquisition among adults, including both heterosexuals and MSM. The use of oral antiretrovirals to prevent HIV infection among HIV-negative MSM has been shown to be safe and effective. A large, randomized, placebo-controlled trial demonstrated a 44% reduction in HIV incidence among MSM receiving daily oral fixed-dose tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine (Truvada) in combination with an HIV prevention package. Improved protection was observed with higher adherence levels. PrEP is indicated for HIV-negative MSM at high risk for HIV acquisition who are willing and motivated to use PrEP as part of a comprehensive HIV prevention package, including condoms, lubrication, STI management, and risk reduction counseling. Baseline investigations should include HIV testing, creatinine clearance estimation, and STI and hepatitis B screening. Eligible MSM can be prescribed daily oral Truvada with adherence support. PrEP should not be given to MSM with abnormal renal function, those unmotivated to use PrEP as part of an HIV prevention package, or during acute viral illnesses. Regular follow-up visits are recommended to assess tolerance, renal function, adherence, and ongoing eligibility. The HIV epidemic continues to spread among gay, bisexual, and other MSM globally. Current HIV prevention strategies are inadequate and insufficiently scaled to control the epidemic. Network-level factors are critically important for HIV spread among MSM. Daily oral PrEP is the only new prevention technology with evidence of efficacy in this population, but its use remains limited, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Expanded use of PrEP and more vigorous prevention efforts are required to reduce new infections among MSM. India has made progress in reducing HIV prevalence, but unprotected sex, commercial sex work, unprotected anal sex between men, and needle sharing among intravenous drug users continue to drive the epidemic. The development of effective, safe, and acceptable topical (microbicides) and oral (PrEP) chemoprophylaxis could augment existing HIV prevention tools. Studies in India show a generally positive attitude toward microbicides and oral PrEP, influenced by factors such as self-perceived HIV risk, product attributes, ease of use, gender norms, and sociocultural context. Further research, including demonstration projects, is needed to assess the acceptability of oral PrEP among high-risk groups. In the UK, professional bodies do not currently recommend PrEP for MSM to prevent HIV acquisition. However, the CDC in the USA has issued interim guidance to facilitate PrEP prescriptions. Disparate international policies can lead to confusing messages for patients seeking information online. A study assessing the quality of internet information available to UK patients about PrEP found that much of the information was not specifically intended for patient use. Improved access to clear and accurate information is needed to support informed decision-making about PrEP.
